question: Your patient just came back from abdominal surgery. Their tummy feels a bit swollen and you can't hear any bowel sounds. What is the best nursing action?

options.A: Administer a strong laxative orally right away
options.B: Massage the abdomen vigorously to force gas out
options.C: Encourage the patient to eat a large solid meal
options.D: Keep the patient NPO until bowel activity returns

explanation: If the bowel isn't moving (paralytic ileus), giving food or drink will only cause nausea and vomiting. Keeping them NPO (nothing by mouth) keeps them safe until peristalsis wakes up!

question: What is the main reason for using a uterine sound before IUD insertion?

options.A: To numb the inside of the uterus against cramps
options.B: To measure how deep and in which direction the uterus goes
options.C: To clean out blood and mucus from the canal
options.D: To widen the vagina so the speculum opens wider

explanation: Sounding gives you an exact measurement of the uterine depth, making sure you don't push the IUD in too far and cause a perforation.

question: When does the debriefing session take place in the simulation learning cycle?

options.A: Before the students even read their patient charts
options.B: Immediately after the simulation scenario finishes
options.C: Only when a student fails a practical examination
options.D: Several weeks after the clinical rotation is finished

explanation: Debriefing happens right after the scenario while the events and emotions are still fresh in the students' minds. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T8#GNS212_U4_T8_h5)

question: What is spermatogenesis?

options.A: The release of seminal fluid during ejaculation
options.B: The storage of mature sperm inside the epididymis
options.C: The hormonal control of secondary sex characteristics
options.D: The production of mature sperm cells from primitive germ cells

explanation: Spermatogenesis describes the biological creation and development of mature sperm cells from immature precursors in the testes. [learn more](GNS216_U2_T7#GNS216_U2_T7_h1)

question: A local health clinic places its mobile immunization teams in hard-to-reach nomadic settlements instead of the well-served town center. Which PHC principle is this?

options.A: Intersectoral cost-sharing
options.B: Equity and social justice
options.C: High-tech specialization
options.D: Centralized medical control

explanation: Spot on! Taking services directly to vulnerable, hard-to-reach groups is the true definition of equity in action.

question: What can happen if a nurse rudely dismisses a patient for using traditional local remedies?

options.A: The hospital will automatically discharge the patient for misconduct
options.B: Local herbalists will protest outside the hospital gates
options.C: The patient will instantly abandon all traditional beliefs forever
options.D: The patient may hide information or delay seeking crucial medical help

explanation: Spot on. Harsh judgments push patients away, making them hide vital health info or avoid getting help when they need it most.

question: When a baby's head is nicely tucked with the chin to the chest, what is the measurement of the suboccipito-bregmatic diameter?

options.D: 9.5 cm

explanation: When the baby tucks its chin right into its chest, it presents its smallest and best measurement for birth: 9.5 centimeters. Beautiful design by nature!

question: As a nurse working in adolescent health, which of these actions should you definitely NOT do?

options.A: Sharing a teenager's private health details with their neighbors
options.B: Screening for risky behaviors in a supportive, private setting
options.C: Providing confidential counseling on sexually transmitted infections
options.D: Educating on the correct use of modern contraceptive methods

explanation: Patient confidentiality is sacred! Gossiping or sharing private health info breaks professional ethics and destroys patient trust immediately.

question: What are the main warning signs of severe pre-eclampsia during pregnancy?

options.A: Complete cessation of fetal movements felt by the mother for two days
options.B: Very high blood pressure accompanied by severe headache and visual changes
options.C: Sudden painless vaginal bleeding in the third trimester of pregnancy
options.D: High fever with generalized body chills and offensive vaginal discharge

explanation: Always watch out for high blood pressure paired with stubborn headaches or blurred vision—these are big red flags for pre-eclampsia!

question: A patient feels very embarrassed and down about sexual changes after prostate surgery. How should you respond as a nurse?

options.A: Acknowledge his feelings and offer a supportive, nonjudgmental space to discuss concerns
options.B: Tell him that sexual function is entirely unimportant compared to curing his urinary obstruction
options.C: Advise him to immediately stop taking all prescribed postoperative medications
options.D: Assure him that normal function always returns within twenty-four hours

explanation: Being heard and accepted with empathy helps patients cope with sensitive body-image and emotional challenges after major surgery.

question: A client considering a tubal ligation is worried it will ruin her sex life and stop her periods. What should you tell her?

options.A: Explain that the surgery only blocks the tubes and does not affect hormones, sexual desire, or menstrual cycles
options.B: Agree that she will enter early menopause and lose all sexual interest immediately
options.C: Tell her that her periods will stop completely because her ovaries will be removed
options.D: Suggest she use emergency contraceptive pills instead of surgery forever

explanation: As a nurse, part of your job is reassurance! Tubal ligation only blocks the path for the egg and sperm; her ovaries stay safe and keep producing her normal hormones.

question: What is a major long-term complication caused by damage to the bladder during a gishiri cut?

options.A: Vesicovaginal fistula
options.B: Gestational diabetes
options.C: Pelvic organ prolapse
options.D: Chronic hypertension

explanation: A vesicovaginal fistula is an abnormal opening between the bladder and vagina that results in continuous urinary incontinence. [learn more](GNS312_U1_T16#GNS312_U1_T16_h4)

question: What are vital statistics primarily records of?

options.A: Life events in a human population
options.B: Financial budgets of local clinics
options.C: Hospital equipment inventory
options.D: Nursing school enrollment numbers

explanation: Vital statistics focus strictly on tracking core life events such as births, deaths, and marriages within a community. [learn more](GNS313_U4_T2#GNS313_U4_T2_h1)

question: Why is it usually unhelpful to just blame an individual nurse when an error occurs?

options.A: It ignores the deeper system and workflow flaws that caused the error
options.B: Individual mistakes never actually lead to serious patient injuries
options.C: Nurses are protected by law from ever making mistakes
options.D: Blaming workers makes hospital administrators work much slower

explanation: Fixing bad workflows stops future mistakes. Just blaming a person doesn't change the unsafe conditions they had to work in.

question: What is the main job of hepatocytes inside the liver?

options.A: Producing red blood cells
options.B: Handling metabolism and clearing out toxins
options.C: Pumping oxygenated blood into the systemic circulation
options.D: Filtering waste through the kidneys

explanation: Hepatocytes are the hardworking main cells of the liver. They manage your metabolism, build proteins, and clear out body toxins every single day!

question: How do somatic motor pathways typically reach their target muscles?

options.A: They operate completely without you ever knowing
options.B: They use a two-neuron chain with a ganglion in the middle
options.C: They only stimulate internal glands and organs
options.D: They use a single direct neuron straight to the muscle

explanation: That's right! Somatic pathways take a straight, fast path from the spinal cord straight to the skeletal muscle with no stops in between.

question: What injection must be given to an Rh-negative mother after a miscarriage to protect her future pregnancies?

options.A: Oxytocin injection
options.B: Broad-spectrum antibiotic
options.C: Iron supplement syrup
options.D: RhoGAM (Rh immunoglobulin)

explanation: RhoGAM stops an Rh-negative mother's body from forming antibodies that could attack the blood of future babies. Brilliant nursing knowledge to keep in mind!

question: What is the main goal behind how an operating room is designed?

options.A: Minimizing infection risk and keeping patients safe
options.B: Allowing family members to watch procedures
options.C: Speeding up the recovery time after surgery
options.D: Reducing the cost of surgical instruments

explanation: Spot on! Everything in the operating room layout is carefully planned to keep the area sterile and protect our patients from infections. You've got this!

question: In Social Cognitive Theory, what do we mean by 'self-efficacy'?

options.A: A doctor's skill in diagnosing lifestyle diseases
options.B: The rate at which a community accepts new public health laws
options.C: A person's belief in their ability to succeed in performing a specific task
options.D: The financial cost required to maintain a healthy diet

explanation: Well done! Self-efficacy is simply your confidence in your own ability to pull off a specific action or goal.

question: Which of these is a dangerous mistake during an emergency obstetric triage?

options.A: Notifying the medical doctor immediately upon finding abnormal bleeding
options.B: Placing an unstable patient in a quiet resuscitation bay
options.C: Delaying vital sign assessment to fill out admission paperwork
options.D: Checking maternal blood pressure upon entry

explanation: Never let paperwork delay patient care! In emergencies, checking vital signs and stabilizing the patient comes first.

question: Which of these makes a urinary tract infection automatically classified as 'complicated'?

options.A: The patient is a non-pregnant adult female
options.B: The infection occurs in a male patient
options.C: Urinalysis shows trace amounts of blood
options.D: Symptoms started less than 24 hours ago

explanation: Because of male anatomy and possible prostate involvement, any UTI in a male is automatically treated as complicated.

question: What is the main risk of having metal pins go through the scalp into the skull bone?

options.A: Permanent hair loss across the forehead
options.B: Local infection and bone inflammation
options.C: Sudden increase in blood pressure
options.D: Complete loss of the sense of smell

explanation: Anytime the skin is broken by metal pins, bacteria can sneak in, making infection our top worry to watch out for.

question: What do we call a 'near miss' in the hospital?

options.A: An error that is caught before it reaches or harms the patient
options.B: A patient complaint about long waiting times at the clinic
options.C: A minor side effect of a drug that was expected by the doctor
options.D: An adverse event that causes permanent physical disability

explanation: Spot on! A near miss is a lucky save where a mistake almost happened, but someone caught it right on time before the patient got hurt.

question: What does 'capacity building' by an NGO usually look like in a community?

options.A: Auditing government financial accounts annually
options.B: Replacing all doctors with foreign medical specialists
options.C: Constructing large teaching hospitals in major capital cities
options.D: Training local volunteers and birth attendants to educate communities

explanation: Capacity building is all about empowering locals! By teaching community members new skills, health programs can keep running long after the NGO leaves.

question: Why is it so important for nurses to directly ask new mothers about leakage or pain during postnatal visits?

options.A: Hospital policy requires a written confession of any weakness
options.B: Postnatal hormones cause temporary memory loss regarding physical symptoms
options.C: Midwives are legally forbidden from physical examinations without questions first
options.D: Patients often feel embarrassed to bring up issues like leakage or pain on their own

explanation: Spot on! Many women suffer quietly because they think postpartum leaking is just 'normal now'. As nurses, we must gently check in on them.

question: What was the main characteristic of the health care model before the Alma-Ata conference?

options.A: It relied entirely on traditional herbal practitioners in rural areas
options.B: It focused primarily on community-based disease prevention
options.C: It was heavily curative and concentrated in urban hospitals
options.D: It provided free universal insurance for all citizens equally

explanation: Before Alma-Ata, global health systems focused on treating sick patients in city-based hospitals rather than preventing disease in communities. [learn more](GNS124_U1_T2#GNS124_U1_T2_h2)

question: A patient repeatedly visits the emergency ward with vague abdominal pain and bruises, but avoids eye contact and looks at her partner before answering questions. What should the nurse suspect?

options.A: Severe dietary deficiency causing weak blood vessels
options.B: Intentional fabrication of symptoms to get medicine
options.C: A rare genetic disorder causing spontaneous bruising
options.D: Underlying gender-based violence and control

explanation: Recurrent injuries combined with controlling partner behavior are classic warning signs of domestic abuse. [learn more](GNS312_U4_T12#GNS312_U4_T12_h3)

question: Why are abstinence-only education programs often insufficient for protecting teenagers?

options.A: They force schools to close down health clinics
options.B: They cause physical delays in the maturation of the prefrontal cortex
options.C: They encourage teenagers to read explicit material online instead
options.D: They fail to give youth who become active the practical skills needed to prevent diseases and pregnancies

explanation: While abstinence is important, withholding practical information about contraception leaves sexually active teens completely unprotected. [learn more](GNS312_U3_T9#GNS312_U3_T9_h8)

question: Which of these is NOT a rule for the lactational amenorrhea method (LAM) to work as birth control?

options.A: The infant must be over one year old
options.B: The baby must be under six months of age
options.C: The mother's menses must not have returned
options.D: The mother must exclusively breastfeed

explanation: LAM only works for babies under six months old who are exclusively breastfed and whose monthly periods have not returned yet.

question: What must you do if a labouring woman's progress on the partograph crosses over the action line?

options.A: Take immediate steps for intervention and management
options.B: Discharge the patient home for rest
options.C: Wait another four hours without changes
options.D: Switch from monitoring vitals to once daily

explanation: Spot on! Crossing the action line is a clear warning sign that labour isn't going as smoothly as expected, so prompt medical action is required to help mother and baby.

question: What is the most common early sign of endometrial cancer?

options.A: Postmenopausal vaginal bleeding
options.B: Swelling in both lower legs
options.C: Severe lower back pain
options.D: Rapid unintended weight loss

explanation: You nailed it! Any bleeding or spotting after menopause is a red flag that always needs a doctor's attention.

question: A patient with a history of a previous heart attack is receiving counseling on diet and taking prescribed statins. Which level of prevention does this care represent?

options.A: Primary prevention
options.B: Tertiary prevention
options.C: Secondary prevention
options.D: Quaternary prevention

explanation: Secondary prevention focuses on early diagnosis, prompt medical treatment, and lifestyle changes to halt disease progression in someone who already has a condition. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T15#GNS213_U1_T15_h1)

question: Why must we strictly isolate confirmed patients during a viral hemorrhagic fever outbreak?

options.A: To break the chain of direct transmission
options.B: To punish patients for contracting the virus
options.C: To reduce the cost of hospital medications
options.D: To simplify hospital administrative paperwork

explanation: You got it! Isolating infected patients keeps the virus away from healthy people and successfully stops the spread.

question: Why do toxins breathed into the lungs (inhalation) affect the body so quickly?

options.A: The stomach acid breaks down inhaled gases faster than swallowed solids
options.B: Skin pores open wider when toxic fumes are breathed into the room
options.C: Inhaled toxins must first pass through the liver before reaching the brain
options.D: Gases pass directly from the lung alveoli into the rich capillary blood supply

explanation: Think about the tiny air sacs (alveoli) in our lungs—they have a massive blood supply, letting gases jump straight into the bloodstream almost instantly!

question: Why should hospital waste bags be tied up when they are only three-quarters full?

options.A: To ensure the waste weighs exactly the same as household garbage
options.B: To prevent overfilling, tearing, and accidental spills during transit
options.C: To give the cleaning staff enough time to take a lunch break
options.D: To allow the municipal collection agency to charge lower fees

explanation: Exactly! Leaving a bit of space at the top lets you tie the bag securely and stops nasty spills on the way out.

question: What is the name of the special, yellowish first milk produced right after birth?

options.A: Lochia
options.B: Meconium
options.C: Serum
options.D: Colostrum

explanation: You got it! Colostrum is nature's gold for the baby—packed with antibodies and protein to protect the newborn and kickstart their digestion.

question: What is the term for a permanent alteration in the DNA sequence?

options.A: A mutation
options.B: A karyotype
options.C: A replication
options.D: A translation

explanation: A mutation is any change in the normal sequence of DNA nucleotides. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T7#GNS111_U1_T7_h5)

question: Why is this special fund called 'revolving'?

options.A: Prices of medicines rotate every week based on inflation
options.B: Doctors take turns managing the pharmacy key
options.C: Patients return unsold drugs to get their money back
options.D: Money from drug sales is used to purchase replacement stock

explanation: Think of it as a cycle! Cash turns into drugs, drugs turn into cash, and the process keeps turning or 'revolving' so the pharmacy always has stock.

question: What usually happens if a patient accidentally swallows a sublingual tablet with water?

options.A: The drug will turn into a toxic substance in the intestines.
options.B: The drug may be destroyed by stomach acid and liver enzymes.
options.C: There will be no change in how the drug works.
options.D: The drug will absorb twice as fast through the stomach lining.

explanation: Correct! Swallowing it means it faces stomach acid and the liver, which can weaken or destroy the drug before it works.

question: Why is spotting patient risks early considered a protective action?

options.A: It guarantees the patient will never experience an infection
options.B: It allows nurses to build barriers against potential hazards
options.C: It removes all clinical responsibilities from the doctor
options.D: It stops patients from moving around the ward

explanation: Spotting risks beforehand lets you put preventative steps in place before an accident or complication actually happens. You've got this!

question: How does spacing children properly help a mother's health?

options.A: It guarantees an easier delivery without any pain management
options.B: It lowers the risks of pregnancy complications and maternal death
options.C: It speeds up the physical aging process of reproductive organs
options.D: It permanently eliminates all future risks of chronic illness

explanation: Giving the body enough time to recover between pregnancies helps prevent severe exhaustion and bleeding, keeping mums safe and healthy!

question: What is the main job of the three tiny bones in the middle ear?

options.A: Produce cerumen to trap foreign bodies
options.B: Amplify and transmit sound vibrations
options.C: Drain excess fluid from the inner ear
options.D: Maintain balance and body posture

explanation: Meet the malleus, incus, and stapes! They take the vibrations from your eardrum, boost their volume, and pass them deeper into the ear.

question: A nurse manager focuses only on cutting hospital operational costs while the ward nurses focus on getting overtime pay. What does this situation highlight?

options.A: A complete absence of any nursing documentation
options.B: That organisational objectives and personal objectives are always identical
options.C: That nurses do not care about patient care at all
options.D: A difference in focus between organisational and personal objectives

explanation: Management looks at the facility's budget (organisational), while staff nurses look at their own earnings and welfare (personal). Their focus is simply different here!

question: Which cranial nerves are attached to the medulla oblongata?

options.A: CN V, VI, VII, and VIII
options.B: CN IX, X, XI, and XII
options.C: CN III, IV, V, and VI
options.D: CN I, II, III, and IV

explanation: The glossopharyngeal, vagus, accessory, and hypoglossal cranial nerves all have their roots emerging from the medulla. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T21#GNS211_U3_T21_h2)

question: What is the job of the obturator in a tracheostomy kit?

options.A: To collect thick mucus from the lungs
options.B: To secure the ties around the patient's neck
options.C: To inflate and deflate the tracheal cuff
options.D: To guide smooth insertion of the tube without injury

explanation: Think of the obturator as a smooth guide! Its rounded tip helps slide the tracheostomy tube right into place without scratching the tissue.

question: A patient develops a sudden, severe facial swelling and rash immediately after starting a new antibiotic. What is the most appropriate nursing action?

options.A: Reassure the patient that rashes are normal and tell them to finish the drug
options.B: Double the fluid intake and ask the patient to sleep off the swelling
options.C: Wait until the next scheduled outpatient clinic visit to mention the rash
options.D: Stop the drug immediately, notify the prescriber, and submit an adverse reaction report

explanation: Signs of a severe allergic reaction require immediate cessation of the offending drug, medical notification, and formal reporting. [learn more](GNS223_U3_T9#GNS223_U3_T9_h6)

question: What causes the yellowish skin color seen in neonatal jaundice?

options.A: An excess of white blood cells in the bloodstream
options.B: A temporary infection of the newborn's liver
options.C: Low levels of iron stored in newborn tissues
options.D: The accumulation of bilirubin in the body

explanation: Bilirubin is a yellow pigment produced when red blood cells break down, and it builds up in the skin and eyes when the baby's body cannot clear it fast enough. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T017#GNS226_U3_T017_h1)

question: What is a major goal of community blood pressure screening programs?

options.A: To distribute free surgical equipment to local residents
options.B: To diagnose and treat rare genetic skin disorders
options.C: To replace hospital emergency rooms entirely
options.D: To identify undiagnosed hypertension early before complications occur

explanation: You got it! Since hypertension is 'silent,' community screenings help catch it early so we can prevent strokes and heart attacks.

question: A patient comes to the clinic with joint pain and a rash two weeks after receiving horse serum for a snakebite. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.A: A normal side effect of venom
options.B: An acute anaphylactic shock
options.C: Serum sickness
options.D: A bacterial wound infection

explanation: Spot on! The 1 to 3 week timeline plus exposure to animal-based treatment is a textbook picture of serum sickness.

question: What do we call the fraction of a drug that successfully reaches the bloodstream in an active, unchanged form?

options.A: Clearance rate
options.B: Half-life
options.C: Bioavailability
options.D: Volume of distribution

explanation: Bioavailability simply means 'how much active drug is actually available' to your body to do its job after the journey.

question: The chest electrodes on an ECG mainly give us a great look at which part of the heart?

options.A: The left ventricle
options.B: The right atrium
options.C: The inferior vena cava
options.D: The sinoatrial node

explanation: The chest leads (V1 to V6) wrap around the front to give us a clear window into the hardworking left ventricle.

question: How should a nurse talk to a patient about their use of local herbal mixtures to ensure safety?

options.A: Ignoring home remedies to focus solely on orthodox hospital drugs
options.B: Telling the patient immediately that all local herbs are dangerous poison
options.C: Reporting the patient to hospital security for using unapproved substances
options.D: Asking calm, non-judgmental questions about all home remedies used

explanation: Wonderful! Being open and non-judgmental builds trust, making patients feel safe to share what they are taking.

question: Why must you record it carefully when a client decides to switch their contraceptive method?

options.A: To prove that the previous contraceptive method caused a severe illness
options.B: To calculate the exact daily financial income generated by the clinic
options.C: To prevent inaccurate tallying and avoid double-counting service statistics
options.D: To satisfy legal requirements for changing a patient's legal surname

explanation: You got it! Tracking method switches properly keeps our numbers honest and stops us from accidentally counting the same person twice.

question: Which simple tool do nurses commonly use to screen adult patients for distant vision problems?

options.A: Otoscope
options.B: Snellen chart
options.C: Ophthalmoscope
options.D: Tuning fork

explanation: The Snellen chart is the classic eye chart with rows of letters that we use to check how clearly someone can see from a distance. Great clinical tool to keep in mind!

question: Why do patients with sickle cell anaemia often have chronic jaundice (yellow eyes and skin)?

options.A: The rapid destruction of fragile sickled red blood cells releases excess bilirubin
options.B: The liver fails to produce enough bile salts for normal digestion
options.C: Chronic low-grade kidney failure traps yellow waste products in the skin
options.D: Blocked blood vessels in the pancreas cause a backup of digestive enzymes

explanation: Think of it this way: sickle cells break down much faster than normal round red blood cells. This rapid breakdown releases a lot of bilirubin into the blood faster than the liver can clear it, turning the skin and eyes yellow.

question: Which of the following is a common physical risk factor for sexual dysfunction?

options.A: Diabetes mellitus
options.B: Drinking adequate water
options.C: Regular aerobic exercise
options.D: Eating fresh fruits daily

explanation: Chronic conditions like diabetes damage blood vessels and nerves over time, making it a major physical risk factor for sexual dysfunction. [learn more](GNS312_U1_T26#GNS312_U1_T26_h3)

question: Why do we ask a patient to empty their bladder right before a proctoscopy?

options.A: To activate systemic blood pressure medications
options.B: To reduce pelvic pressure and enhance comfort
options.C: To prevent sudden urinary tract infections
options.D: To collect a routine clean-catch urine specimen

explanation: That's correct! An empty bladder takes up less room in the pelvis, which leaves more space and makes the exam much more comfortable for the patient.

question: A nurse wants to improve maternal health in a rural area where many women use traditional birth attendants. What is the best approach regarding these attendants?

options.A: Ignore them completely and tell pregnant women never to speak to them
options.B: Ask them to close their businesses and work as hospital cleaners
options.C: Arrest them immediately for practicing medicine without a formal license
options.D: Engage and train them to recognize danger signs and refer women to the clinic

explanation: Working with traditional birth attendants builds a safe bridge instead of creating conflict, saving more mothers. [learn more](GNS124_U4_T1#GNS124_U4_T1_h4)

question: What is an essential nursing duty when caring for a patient with acute poisoning?

options.A: Leaving the patient alone to rest quietly in a dark room
options.B: Gathering the history, securing samples, and keeping the bedside safe
options.C: Disposing of all empty medication containers immediately
options.D: Prescribing the final discharge medications without doctor review

explanation: Nurses act as detectives! Collecting pill bottles, noting what was taken, and keeping the patient safe from harm are key parts of emergency care.

question: A young student in Nigeria worries that taking Postinor-2 will make her barren. How should you respond?

options.A: Prescribe a strong surgical procedure to clear her reproductive system
options.B: Scold her for engaging in premarital sex and refuse to give her the medication
options.C: Gently educate her with facts, explaining that the drug does not cause permanent infertility
options.D: Agree with her fears and advise her never to use any form of family planning

explanation: Market myths can be scary! Gently talking clients through the facts builds trust and ensures they get safe, accurate reproductive healthcare. You're going to be an amazing nurse!

question: Which of these is NOT a negative consequence of child marriage for a young girl?

options.A: Severe psychological trauma and social isolation
options.B: Permanent immunity against sexually transmitted infections
options.C: High risk of early adolescent pregnancy complications
options.D: Abrupt termination of her formal education

explanation: Correct! Child marriage definitely does not grant immunity to infections; starting sexual activity early often raises that risk instead.

question: Which specific protein found in grains triggers the immune reaction that damages the small intestine in celiac disease?

options.A: Albumin
options.B: Lactose
options.C: Gluten
options.D: Casein

explanation: Gluten is the protein in wheat, barley, and rye that sets off the immune response in celiac disease. You've got this!

question: When is an antiarrhythmic drug like amiodarone usually given during resuscitation?

options.A: For persistent shockable rhythms like ventricular fibrillation
options.B: As the first medication before any chest compressions begin
options.C: To treat severe sinus bradycardia and low blood pressure
options.D: To reverse respiratory depression caused by opioid overdose

explanation: We pull out amiodarone when electric shocks and CPR haven't quite managed to fix stubborn rhythms like V-fib yet.

question: What is the main job of sensory receptors in our special senses?

options.A: Pump blood through the sensory organs
options.B: Convert environmental stimuli into electrical signals
options.C: Store memories of past sensory experiences
options.D: Produce hormones to regulate body temperature

explanation: Think of sensory receptors as tiny translators! They take physical things from the world around us—like light or sound—and change them into electrical signals that our nervous system can easily read and understand.

question: Why is teaching patients how to avoid environmental hazards so important after an insect sting recovery?

options.A: It guarantees that insect populations will decrease around the home
options.B: It eliminates the patient's biological sensitivity to insect venom
options.C: It minimizes the chance of future exposure and repeat anaphylactic events
options.D: It replaces the need to carry emergency rescue medications

explanation: Prevention is key! Simple steps like wearing protective clothes keep patients out of harm's way so they don't experience another scary reaction.

question: Why is a bedside double-check with two nurses a must before starting a blood transfusion?

options.A: To make sure the nurse finishes the shift on time
options.B: To prevent fatal errors by confirming exact patient and blood product matching
options.C: To measure the exact weight of the blood bag before hanging
options.D: To ensure the blood pump is plugged into a backup generator

explanation: Two pairs of eyes are better than one! Checking details together ensures the right blood goes to the right patient every single time.

question: What does health literacy refer to in nursing practice?

options.A: The number of medical books a patient has read at home
options.B: A person's ability to understand and use basic health information
options.C: How fast a client can write down their doctor's name
options.D: The level of education the nurse completed in school

explanation: Health literacy is the practical skill of understanding medical instructions, prescriptions, and health advice. [learn more](GNS125_U3_T3#GNS125_U3_T3_h3)

question: What is an obstetric fistula?

options.A: A permanent infection of the surgical wound after a caesarean section
options.B: A complete blockage of the fallopian tubes caused by gonorrhea
options.C: A chronic weakness of the heart muscle following severe pre-eclampsia
options.D: An abnormal hole between the birth canal and bladder or rectum

explanation: Obstetric fistula happens when prolonged pressure during obstructed labor damages tissue, creating an unwanted opening that leads to continuous leakage. Compassionate nursing care is vital here.

question: Why does a mother's heart output temporarily spike during a contraction in labour?

options.A: The baby pushes directly against the mother's main heart valves
options.B: The mother hyperventilates to increase her oxygen levels
options.C: Uterine contractions release massive amounts of adrenaline
options.D: Blood is squeezed out of the placenta and back into maternal circulation

explanation: You're learning fast! Each contraction pushes pooled blood out of the womb and back into the mother's general circulation.

question: In a busy clinic, how does a multi-dose medication vial usually get contaminated?

options.A: Using a previously used needle or syringe to enter the vial
options.B: Cleaning the rubber stopper with alcohol before every puncture
options.C: Storing the medicine bottle inside a warm medication refrigerator
options.D: Failing to shake the suspension liquid before drawing a dose

question: What is the main goal of family planning in public health?

options.A: Allowing individuals to choose the timing and spacing of children
options.B: Forcing families to limit their total number of offspring to two
options.C: Eliminating population growth completely across all developing nations
options.D: Providing free medical care exclusively for newborn infants

explanation: You got it! Family planning is all about giving people the freedom to decide when and how often to have children, which keeps both parents and babies healthy.

question: A patient complains of severe stomach pain. What does a nurse with strong analytical skills do first?

options.A: Give the strongest pain medication available immediately
options.B: Discharge the patient because pain scales are unreliable
options.C: Tell the patient that stomach pain is normal after surgery
options.D: Check surgical history, lab results, and current medications

explanation: Analytical skills help the nurse look at multiple data sources to understand the root cause before acting. [learn more](GNS112_U3_T7#GNS112_U3_T7_h3)

question: Which of these details is NOT necessary to write down in your notes after a blood transfusion?

options.A: The name of the blood donor's family members
options.B: The product serial number and volume given
options.C: The start and stop times of the infusion
options.D: The patient's post-transfusion vital signs

explanation: Donor privacy is key! Blood banks keep donor details strictly confidential, so they never appear in your patient's chart.

question: Why might a patient with a left atrial myxoma suddenly faint when changing body position?

options.A: The tumour causes a sudden drop in the patient's body temperature
options.B: The heart muscle instantly grows twice its normal size
options.C: The mobile tumour temporarily plugs up the mitral valve, stopping blood flow
options.D: The patient's lungs stop taking in oxygen due to an allergic reaction

explanation: Some tumours hang on a little stalk. When the patient moves, the tumour can swing over and block the valve like a cork in a bottle, cutting off blood supply and causing fainting. Fascinating clinical detail!

question: What does patient autonomy mean in the context of home health care?

options.A: The legal obligation of the family to pay for all medical supplies
options.B: The requirement for patients to live completely independently
options.C: The authority of the nurse to override family member requests
options.D: The right of the patient to make their own choices about care

explanation: Autonomy refers to a patient's right to self-determination and making personal decisions regarding their treatment plan. [learn more](GNS324_U1_T7#GNS324_U1_T7_h7)

question: Which emotional reaction is very common in patients right after they acquire a physical disability?

options.A: Complete indifference and forgetfulness
options.B: Grief, shock, and depression
options.C: Aggressive pursuit of extreme sports
options.D: Immediate acceptance and joy

explanation: Losing bodily function triggers a deep grief process, much like losing a loved one. Shock and depression are very normal initial responses.

question: A patient is brought to the ward in a deep coma after a severe head injury. Which nursing action is best to prevent stiff joints?

options.A: Doing regular passive range of motion exercises
options.B: Encouraging the client to squeeze rubber balls daily
options.C: Tying all four limbs tightly to the bed rails
options.D: Putting heavy sandbags on the hands and feet

explanation: Brilliant! An unconscious client cannot move on their own, so scheduled passive range of motion keeps their joints mobile and safe.

question: Which gland pumps adrenaline (epinephrine) straight into the blood during a scare?

options.A: Thyroid gland
options.B: Pancreas
options.C: Adrenal medulla
options.D: Pituitary gland

explanation: The inner part of your adrenal gland (the medulla) acts fast, releasing epinephrine into the bloodstream to back up your nervous system during a rush.

question: Which of these is a major social root cause of family vulnerability?

options.A: Attending religious gatherings very often
options.B: Living right next to a teaching hospital
options.C: Economic instability and chronic poverty
options.D: Having many healthy children at home

explanation: Exactly! Poverty strips families of the financial cushion they need to buy food, secure good housing, and pay for hospital bills when sickness strikes.

question: What is an important nursing duty before an endoscopy procedure begins?

options.A: Ensuring the informed consent form is signed and placed in the chart
options.B: Prescribing the specific dose of sedative drugs for the doctor
options.C: Repairing any broken fibre-optic cables on the camera
options.D: Performing the actual surgical scope insertion in the clinic

explanation: As a nurse, we double-check that the doctor has explained everything and that the signed consent form is safely in the patient's records before they go in.

question: What is a big plus of using a flexible fiberoptic scope instead of a rigid one in the clinic?

options.A: The patient can remain awake and talk while vocal cord movement is assessed.
options.B: It completely eliminates any risk of a patient gagging during the test.
options.C: It provides a wider surgical field for removing large vocal cord tumors.
options.D: It requires full general anesthesia to relax the throat muscles completely.

explanation: Exactly! Because the patient is awake, doctors can actually watch how the vocal cords move when they talk or breathe.

question: Why does the Basel Convention emphasize stopping waste creation right at the source?

options.A: International shipping companies refuse to carry heavy metal byproducts
options.B: Preventing waste creation is safer than trying to manage it later
options.C: Governments want to completely shut down the chemical manufacturing sector
options.D: It is cheaper to burn hazardous waste in city centers than transport it

explanation: Makes total sense, right? If you don't create the toxic byproduct in the first place, you completely avoid the risks of transporting and disposing of it.

question: How should you position an adult patient's pinna to straighten their ear canal before looking inside?

options.A: Upward and forward
options.B: Straight down
options.C: Upward and backward
options.D: Downward and forward

explanation: For adults, pulling the pinna upward and backward straightens out that natural S-curve of the ear canal so you can see clearly.

question: Why are community health workers so helpful in managing family planning defaulters?

options.A: They manufacture all contraceptive drugs locally
options.B: They possess the legal power to arrest clients who miss appointments
options.C: They replace the need for physical clinics entirely
options.D: They can bridge the gap by reaching clients who cannot travel to the clinic

explanation: Community health workers extend our reach right into local neighborhoods, helping clients who find it hard to journey to the clinic.

question: What is the main goal of primary health care (PHC) services in Nigeria?

options.A: Handling complex surgical procedures for urban residents
options.B: Conducting advanced medical research in laboratories
options.C: Training international medical specialists
options.D: Bringing essential health services close to the grassroots

explanation: You've got this! Primary health care is all about bringing basic, friendly health services right down to the local communities where everyday people live.

question: What is the main job of a primary health care facility?

options.A: To serve as the first point of contact for community health needs
options.B: To train resident doctors and medical specialists
options.C: To provide long-term care for chronic psychiatric disorders
options.D: To perform major surgical operations like brain surgery

explanation: Primary health centers are right there in the community. They are the friendly first stop for everyday health needs and prevention.

question: Which patient group requires the greatest caution when taking anticholinergic medications?

options.A: Older adult patients
options.B: Young children with fevers
options.C: Pregnant women in their first trimester
options.D: Athletes with muscle sprains

explanation: Older adults are much more sensitive to side effects like confusion, constipation, and urinary retention, increasing complication risks. [learn more](GNS223_U5_T6#GNS223_U5_T6_h6)

question: What is the most important assessment when checking a limb's circulation and nerve function after a joint procedure?

options.A: Measuring the exact circumference of the thigh
options.B: Listening for bowel sounds in the lower abdomen
options.C: Checking the patient's oral temperature reading
options.D: Checking pulse, color, movement, and sensation

explanation: Neurovascular checks (the famous '5 Ps' or pulse, color, movement, and sensation) help you catch any blood flow or nerve issues early before they turn into major complications.

question: A patient with heart failure comes in with swollen legs and shortness of breath. What type of fluid imbalance do they likely have?

options.A: Intracellular dehydration
options.B: Fluid volume excess
options.C: Electrolytes loss only
options.D: Fluid volume deficit

explanation: Exactly! When the heart struggles to pump, the body holds onto extra water and salt, leading to fluid overload and swelling.

question: How does cervical cancer usually develop over time?

options.A: It begins slowly as pre-cancerous cellular changes before invading
options.B: It spreads directly from the ovaries within a few days
options.C: It appears suddenly as a widespread systemic blood infection
options.D: It forms from scar tissue after normal childbirth

explanation: Don't worry, it doesn't happen overnight! It starts with quiet, abnormal cell changes that take years to become true cancer. That is why screening is so powerful.

question: Which Nigerian federal law specifically bans Female Genital Mutilation and punishes offenders?

options.A: Nursing and Midwifery Registration Decree
options.B: Child Nutrition and Immunization Policy
options.C: National Health Insurance Scheme Act
options.D: Violence Against Persons Prohibition (VAPP) Act

explanation: You got it! The VAPP Act of 2015 provides the legal backbone to prosecute anyone performing or promoting FGM in Nigeria.

question: What is another common name for healthcare-associated infections?

options.A: Autoimmune disorders
options.B: Idiopathic conditions
options.C: Nosocomial infections
options.D: Congenital infections

explanation: Nosocomial is the traditional medical term for infections that originate in a hospital environment. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T4#GNS123_U4_T4_h1)

question: A critically ill patient just received a lot of IV fluids. Which sign helps you catch early fluid overload?

options.A: Warm and dry skin on both lower legs
options.B: A slight drop in body temperature
options.C: Developing crackles in the lung bases
options.D: An increase in the patient's daily appetite

explanation: Too much fluid in the system quickly backs up into the lungs, creating those classic crackling sounds when you listen with your stethoscope.

question: How do nurses directly help with cancer epidemiology in clinical and community settings?

options.A: Funding public health research grants through private banks
options.B: Designing blueprints for modern oncology radiation bunkers
options.C: Manufacturing new chemotherapy drugs in hospital pharmacies
options.D: Accurate data collection and maintaining cancer registries

explanation: Nurses play a huge role by gathering precise patient data and keeping records updated, which helps researchers track cancer trends. You're making great progress! [learn more](GNS321_U1_T1#GNS321_U1_T1_h7)

question: What is a major reason why unsafe injections happen in low-resource clinics?

options.A: Having too many nurses on duty at night
options.B: Having way too many sterile water supplies
options.C: Shortages of disposable syringes and safety boxes
options.D: Too many mandatory infection control classes

explanation: When basic supplies run low, healthcare workers are put in tough spots. Advocating for proper supplies is a big part of nursing advocacy.

question: What is the main way Metformin helps lower blood sugar in the body?

options.A: Stimulating the beta cells of the pancreas to release stored insulin
options.B: Slowing down the digestion of carbohydrates in the small intestine
options.C: Decreasing hepatic glucose production and improving insulin sensitivity
options.D: Blocking the reabsorption of glucose in the renal tubules

explanation: Exactly right! Metformin tells the liver to ease up on making extra sugar and helps your body's cells respond better to your natural insulin.

question: Which of these is a great example of a positive feedback loop?

options.A: Insulin lowering high blood sugar back to normal
options.B: Parathyroid hormone raising low blood calcium levels
options.C: Oxytocin increasing uterine contractions during labor
options.D: Thyroid hormone stopping pituitary TSH production

explanation: Positive feedback pushes a process further and faster until the goal is met, just like oxytocin intensifying contractions until baby arrives!

question: A patient states they have smoked for twenty years and wonders if quitting will even help now. What is the most accurate nursing response?

options.A: Smoking only affects your lungs, not your heart or blood vessels
options.B: You must stop all at once without any help or replacement products for it to work
options.C: Quitting will benefit your heart immediately, cutting your heart disease risk in half within one year
options.D: The damage is already permanent, so quitting will not change your risk level

explanation: Cardiovascular benefits begin almost immediately after quitting smoking, and within twelve months, the excess risk of coronary heart disease drops by fifty percent. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T15#GNS213_U1_T15_h5)

question: What is the most common cause of injuries to the brain and spine in our communities?

options.A: Workplace chemical exposure
options.B: Congenital weakness
options.C: Road traffic accidents
options.D: Degenerative joint disease

explanation: You got it! High-speed car and motorcycle crashes unfortunately top the list as the leading cause of traumatic brain and spinal injuries globally.

question: What happens in the kidneys during cystinuria to cause stone formation?

options.A: Rapid enzymatic breakdown of calcium in the glomerulus
options.B: Impaired renal tubular reabsorption of specific amino acids
options.C: Reduced hepatic production of filtering enzymes
options.D: Excessive dietary intake of sulfur-containing proteins

explanation: Think of the kidneys like a recycling plant! In cystinuria, a little genetic mix-up stops the kidneys from reabsorbing certain amino acids back into the body. This causes cystine to build up in the urine and form stones. You've got this!

question: A patient has severe liver disease. Which part of drug processing will most likely be affected?

options.A: Metabolism
options.B: Excretion
options.C: Dissolution
options.D: Absorption

explanation: Spot on! The liver is our main metabolic factory where drugs are broken down and processed.

question: Which group of people often acts as a bridge between local communities and clinical PAC facilities?

options.A: Hospital maintenance staff
options.B: International tax auditors
options.C: Community health workers
options.D: Forensic investigators

explanation: Correct! Community health workers play a wonderful role in guiding patients to local support networks and follow-up care.

question: What is the most important environmental requirement when screening a patient for gender-based violence?

options.A: Absolute privacy away from family members and partners
options.B: Conducting the interview in a busy, open hospital hallway
options.C: The presence of at least three armed security guards
options.D: Having a video camera recording the entire conversation

explanation: Survivors cannot speak freely if the abuser or other family members are present to overhear the discussion. [learn more](GNS312_U4_T12#GNS312_U4_T12_h5)

question: Why might a doctor order an MRI instead of a standard X-ray for a suspected bone injury?

options.A: To measure the exact electrical activity in the bone
options.B: To determine the amount of calcium in the bloodstream
options.C: To detect hidden stress fractures or soft tissue damage
options.D: To check the patient's resting blood pressure levels

explanation: MRIs excel at showing soft tissues like ligaments, tendons, and hairline cracks that standard X-ray beams often miss. [learn more](GNS222_U1_T10#GNS222_U1_T10_h6)

question: What is the quick check a nurse does every time they put on an N95 to check the seal called?

options.A: Qualitative sweet test
options.B: Sterile pressure scan
options.C: Manufacturer inspection
options.D: User seal check

explanation: It is a quick self-check you do every single time you put on your respirator to make sure it is sitting right.

question: Which type of receptor is primarily found on target organs of the parasympathetic nervous system?

options.A: Alpha adrenergic receptors
options.B: Beta adrenergic receptors
options.C: Muscarinic receptors
options.D: Nicotinic skeletal receptors

explanation: Parasympathetic postganglionic fibers release acetylcholine, which binds to muscarinic receptors on target effector organs. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T29#GNS211_U3_T29_h6)

question: What is the term for right-sided heart failure caused by long-term lung disease?

options.A: Cor pulmonale
options.B: Myocardial infarction
options.C: Rheumatic carditis
options.D: Infective endocarditis

explanation: Cor pulmonale refers to enlargement and failure of the right ventricle resulting from high blood pressure in the pulmonary blood vessels due to lung disease. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T8#GNS213_U2_T8_h7)

question: As a registered nurse working under the team nursing model, what is your primary role on the ward?

options.A: Supervising the doctors during ward rounds
options.B: Performing every single procedure personally for all patients
options.C: Handling only the administrative paperwork for the ward
options.D: Acting as the team leader and taking overall accountability

explanation: Spot on! The registered nurse coordinates the group and takes ultimate responsibility for the care given, even when delegating specific tasks to others. You've got this!

question: What is the primary purpose of a gastrostomy feeding tube?

options.A: To deliver nutrition directly into the stomach
options.B: To provide continuous intravenous hydration
options.C: To bypass the small intestine during digestion
options.D: To remove excess air and fluid from the bowel

explanation: A gastrostomy tube places food and fluids straight into the stomach, bypassing the mouth and esophagus for patients who cannot swallow safely. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T4#GNS212_U1_T4_h1)

question: What is the preferred, minimally invasive surgery for stable patients needing a look at their pelvic organs?

options.A: Thoracotomy
options.B: Cystoscopy
options.C: Total hysterectomy
options.D: Laparoscopy

explanation: Spot on! Laparoscopy uses tiny cuts and a camera, meaning less pain and a much faster recovery for the patient.

question: How do hard scars (plaques) cause symptoms in disseminated sclerosis?

options.A: They cause excess production of spinal fluid in the brain ventricles
options.B: They stimulate muscles to contract constantly without rest
options.C: They repair the damaged nerves completely back to normal
options.D: They block and slow down electrical signals traveling along nerve fibers

explanation: When inflammation creates scar tissue (plaques), it gets in the way of smooth electrical conduction—leading to the physical and sensory changes patients feel.

question: Which emotional response is very common in patients who are newly dealing with sensory loss?

options.A: A sudden surge of euphoria and overconfidence
options.B: Aggressive hostility directed exclusively at medical staff
options.C: Grief over lost independence and feelings of isolation
options.D: Complete indifference toward their physical health status

explanation: Losing a sense like sight or hearing is a massive life change. It's completely natural for patients to feel sad, grieve their independence, and feel a bit isolated.

question: What does the letter 'S' stand for twice in the SBAR communication tool?

options.A: Symptom and Staff
options.B: Situation and Assessment
options.C: Support and Solution
options.D: Situation and Safety

explanation: SBAR stands for Situation, Background, Assessment, and Recommendation, which is used for structured clinical handovers. [learn more](GNS225_U3_T15#GNS225_U3_T15_h4)

question: What is the primary effect when significant others view healthcare strictly as a response to severe illness rather than prevention?

options.A: The family will spend excess money on elective wellness check-ups.
options.B: The adolescent will develop an obsession with personal fitness.
options.C: The teenager will independently schedule weekly preventative labs.
options.D: The adolescent will likely skip routine screenings and health checks.

explanation: Household health attitudes shape personal habits; if wellness visits are ignored by family, teenagers rarely seek them out alone. [learn more](GNS312_U3_T20#GNS312_U3_T20_h6)

question: What is the final, essential step when using evaluation data for quality improvement?

options.A: Stopping all routine data collection for the next year
options.B: Punishing staff members whose coverage rates are low
options.C: Filing the completed assessment reports in a locked cabinet
options.D: Implementing corrective actions based on the findings

explanation: Data collection is only useful if we act on it! We must turn our findings into practical changes to improve care for children.

question: What does the tallest bar on a quality improvement chart tracking medication errors signify?

options.A: The medication that is prescribed most accurately
options.B: The average time it takes to process a prescription
options.C: The safest hospital department in the facility
options.D: The category with the highest number of reported errors

explanation: On a frequency bar chart, a taller bar indicates a higher count or greater frequency for that specific category. [learn more](GNS217_U4_T7#GNS217_U4_T7_h5)

question: A nurse notices a 16-year-old girl repeatedly visiting the clinic for minor injuries with vague explanations. What should the nurse do first?

options.A: Scold the patient for being clumsy and failing to take proper precautions
options.B: Report the parents immediately to law enforcement without talking to the teen
options.C: Conduct a private psychosocial assessment using a structured tool like HEADSS
options.D: Discharge the patient quickly so other acute emergency cases can be seen

explanation: Correct! Repeated, unexplained injuries are a major red flag. A private, gentle interview using a tool like HEADSS helps uncover abuse or emotional distress.

question: What is the main goal of secondary prevention in healthcare?

options.A: Enforcing broad national housing and environmental policies
options.B: Rehabilitating patients with long-term physical disabilities
options.C: Completely preventing the initial exposure to a pathogen
options.D: Early diagnosis and prompt treatment of existing disease

explanation: Secondary prevention is all about catching health issues early through screening so we can treat them before they get worse.

question: What tool do managers commonly use to track progress toward objectives?

options.A: Key Performance Indicators (KPIs)
options.B: Random patient complaint letters
options.C: Daily weather forecasts
options.D: Personal diary entries

explanation: KPIs provide measurable data that helps managers track whether goals are being met. [learn more](GST321_U2_T3#GST321_U2_T3_h7)

question: Which of these is a leading direct cause of maternal mortality?

options.A: Benign breast lumps
options.B: Chronic dental caries
options.C: Uncomplicated malaria
options.D: Postpartum hemorrhage

explanation: Heavy bleeding after childbirth is one of the top direct causes of maternal death worldwide. Knowing how to spot and manage it is essential for every nursing student!

question: When amino acids are broken down, they produce toxic ammonia. How does the body safely get rid of it?

options.A: The bone marrow stores it permanently as a solid mineral crystal
options.B: The lungs exhale it immediately as a dry nitrogen gas vapor
options.C: The liver converts it into urea for safe removal by the kidneys
options.D: The stomach uses it directly to neutralize strong gastric acids

explanation: Ammonia is dangerous to our cells, so the liver quickly changes it into a much safer substance called urea. The kidneys then filter this urea out through urine.

question: Which complication frequently develops following prolonged low blood pressure and shock from severe bleeding?

options.A: Acute kidney injury
options.B: Enlargement of the spleen
options.C: Excessive bone mineralization
options.D: Chronic high blood pressure

explanation: When blood flow drops significantly during shock, the kidneys suffer from oxygen deprivation, which can lead to acute kidney damage. [learn more](GNS112_U7_T2#GNS112_U7_T2_h7)

question: Why is the partograph considered such a helpful early warning tool in the labour room?

options.A: It automatically orders emergency caesarean sections from the pharmacy
options.B: It alerts staff to deviations from normal labour before complications become severe
options.C: It predicts the exact gender and birth weight of the baby days in advance
options.D: It rings an electronic alarm bell whenever a contraction starts

explanation: Spotting small changes early makes all the difference. By plotting readings over time, you can catch slow progress or distress early and step in to help.

question: What happens in the body when there is not enough insulin or when insulin doesn't work properly?

options.A: Red blood cells destroy circulating nutrients
options.B: The pancreas stops producing digestive enzymes
options.C: Cells rapidly absorb too much sugar
options.D: Glucose accumulates in the bloodstream

explanation: Without enough working insulin, sugar can't get inside your body's cells for energy, so it builds up in your blood (hyperglycemia). You've got this!

question: Which annoying side effect is very common with ACE inhibitors and often makes patients switch to ARBs?

options.A: Sudden severe hair loss
options.B: Yellowing of the eyes
options.C: Tremors in both hands
options.D: A persistent dry cough

explanation: Spot on! ACE inhibitors can cause a buildup of a substance called bradykinin in the lungs. It's harmless, but that tickly, dry cough can drive patients crazy!

question: What is the main reason we give intermittent preventive treatment (IPTp) for malaria during pregnancy?

options.A: To boost the mother's daily caloric and protein intake
options.B: To prevent the development of gestational diabetes mellitus
options.C: To cure a chronic respiratory infection in the mother
options.D: To reduce placental malaria parasitemia and associated risks

explanation: In malaria-endemic areas like ours, IPTp stops malaria parasites from hiding out in the placenta where they can harm both mother and baby.

question: Why must the rehabilitation nurse involve the patient and family during the goal-setting process?

options.A: To ensure the goals are meaningful and realistic for daily life
options.B: To eliminate the need for physical therapy sessions
options.C: To shift the legal liability of care onto the family members
options.D: To reduce the amount of documentation required in the chart

explanation: When patients and families help create the goals, they are much more motivated to work hard toward achieving them. [learn more](GNS123_U6_T4#GNS123_U6_T4_h2)

question: Why might someone who eats enough food still experience cellular malnutrition?

options.A: They sleep fewer than eight hours every single night
options.B: They are consuming too much water with their meals
options.C: Their stomach physically shrinks from eating at irregular hours
options.D: Their body fails to properly process and utilise the ingested nutrients

explanation: Great thinking! Even with a full plate, cells starve if the body cannot properly break down, transport, or use those nutrients.

question: What is usually the very first sign that a newborn is developing tetanus?

options.A: Yellow discoloration of the skin
options.B: Inability to suck or feed properly
options.C: Total paralysis of the lower limbs
options.D: High fever and watery diarrhea

question: Before puberty starts, what does the central nervous system usually do regarding reproductive hormones?

options.A: It produces excess adult levels
options.B: It completely shuts down the pituitary
options.C: It suppresses hormone release
options.D: It secretes erratic daily spikes

question: What is the big advantage of using a moist cold compress instead of a stiff ice pack?

options.A: They require no refrigeration or ice whatsoever
options.B: They completely eliminate the risk of frostbite
options.C: They mold easily to uneven body contours like the jaw or face
options.D: They stay warm for up to twelve hours at a time

explanation: You got it! Faces and jaws aren't flat, so a flexible moist compress hugs those tricky curves much better than a rigid ice pack.

question: Why does fetal hemoglobin take up oxygen so effectively from maternal blood in the placenta?

options.A: It has a higher affinity for oxygen than adult hemoglobin
options.B: It circulates at a much higher temperature than maternal blood
options.C: It contains more iron atoms per molecule than adult hemoglobin
options.D: It relies on active transport pumps for oxygen molecules

explanation: Fetal hemoglobin grabs onto oxygen more tightly than maternal hemoglobin, allowing it to pull oxygen across the placental membrane successfully. [learn more](GNS121_U6_T7#GNS121_U6_T7_h4)

question: Which chemical exposure patient needs to be rushed straight to the resuscitation bay?

options.A: A patient with normal vital signs and no symptoms
options.B: A patient with abnormal vital signs and respiratory distress
options.C: A calm patient who smelled fumes outside a factory
options.D: A patient with a mild skin redness on one hand

explanation: If vital signs are crashing and the patient is struggling to breathe, they need immediate, high-priority emergency care.

question: Why is it so important to involve the family when setting rehabilitation goals?

options.A: It replaces the need for professional nursing assessments
options.B: It ensures the goals match the patient's real home life
options.C: It forces the family to pay for hospital supplies
options.D: It legally binds the family to provide financial support

explanation: Families know the home environment best. Working together ensures the recovery plan actually makes sense in their daily lives!

question: What physical pressure change forces the foramen ovale to snap shut when a baby is born?

options.A: Direct action of circulating maternal hormones in the blood
options.B: Higher pressure in the left atrium than the right atrium
options.C: Muscular spasms triggered by cold air hitting the skin
options.D: Complete physical scarring of the tissue within seconds

question: During which procedure is the lithotomy position most commonly used?

options.A: Feeding a patient with dysphagia
options.B: Listening to breath sounds in asthma
options.C: Gynecological examinations and childbirth
options.D: Administering a nebulizer treatment

question: Which waste product builds up in the blood to cause hepatic encephalopathy?

options.A: Glucose
options.B: Calcium
options.C: Ammonia
options.D: Sodium

question: An adult patient's calculated BMI is 32.5. How do you classify this using WHO guidelines?

options.A: Obesity Class II

options.C: Obesity Class I
options.D: Severe Obesity
